name: Dr. PRP kit

card.summary: A blood-spinning kit for making platelet-rich plasma, the concentrate injected or microneedled into the scalp or face in hair-thickening and skin-rejuvenation treatments.
card.note: Preparation and injection are clinical procedures; contaminated or reused equipment has caused infections.

quick.overview:
A PRP kit is the tube-and-centrifuge set used to separate platelet-rich plasma from a patient's own blood. This entry covers kits sold under the Dr. PRP name; no manufacturer page could be loaded, so what follows describes PRP kits and the treatment generally.

The appearance payoff is in two areas: hair density and skin quality. Wikipedia reports studies of benefit for androgenetic alopecia and alopecia areata, and PRP is also marketed for wrinkles and skin rejuvenation, including the so-called vampire facial.
quick.how: Blood is drawn, spun in a centrifuge to concentrate platelets to about three to five times normal, then placed back into the scalp or face by injection or alongside microneedling. Hair protocols described on Wikipedia use at least three monthly sessions followed by a maintenance period.
quick.risks: Adverse effects in trials are generally low, but safety depends on how the procedure is done. In 2024 the CDC reported three HIV diagnoses linked to an unlicensed New Mexico spa where blood-contaminated single-use equipment was reused. The FDA clears PRP preparation devices but does not regulate PRP itself.

lead: A PRP kit is a set of tubes, separators and sometimes a centrifuge used to prepare platelet-rich plasma. Wikipedia explains that blood is drawn from the patient and centrifuged to separate the platelet-rich layer, usually in clinics using commercial kits, with results varying between people and facilities. The goal is roughly three to five times the normal platelet concentration [1].

For looks, PRP is used on the scalp for hair thinning and on the face for skin rejuvenation. Studies cited by Wikipedia report benefit in alopecia areata and androgenetic alopecia, including improved hair density and thickness, and PRP is marketed as a minimally invasive treatment for wrinkles and fine lines. "Vampire facials", which combine PRP with microneedling, became popular in the 2010s with celebrity endorsement [1].
Forum members on T Nation mention PRP mostly for joint and tendon problems, and one thread asks whether PRP with growth factors works better than other hair treatments [2][3].

chain: Draw blood and spin it in a kit
Platelet-concentrated plasma is injected or microneedled in
Growth factors act on follicles and skin
Thicker hair or smoother skin texture
angle.text: The kit makes the concentrate; clinicians then apply it to the scalp or face aiming at denser hair or fresher-looking skin.

infobox: Devices need FDA clearance; PRP itself not regulated [1]
At least 3 monthly sessions, then maintenance [1]

paras: PRP is classed by leukocyte and fibrin content into leukocyte-rich PRP, leukocyte-reduced PRP and leukocyte platelet-rich fibrin [1].

Wikipedia reports that PRP may serve as an alternative to minoxidil or finasteride in some studies and that efficacy depends on the number of sessions, single versus double centrifugation, age, sex and injection site [1]. For skin, it is marketed for wrinkles, blemishes and rejuvenation [1].
Adverse effects are generally low in trials. The 2024 New Mexico spa HIV cluster showed that unsafe equipment practices create risk [1].
No studies found of this specific kit. Studies of PRP generally, summarised on Wikipedia, report benefit for hair loss and mixed results across other conditions [1].

timeline.event: The term platelet-rich plasma is first used [1].
Interest in PRP for hair loss begins [1].
